comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
Sure, but you've abandoned Gwern's point now. Retreating from the motte will save your face but only by leaving Gwern out in the cold.

Consider the weather. Imperfect prediction of the weather has transformed society (and "the economy", whatever the fuck that is), but perfect prediction of the weather is impossible. The relevant limitation here is chaotic; even if we knew the positions of all atoms in the atmosphere, we will eventually be overwhelmed by the numerical effects of chaos. As a result, weather prediction beyond about two weeks is not physically realizable, regardless of implementation strategy. This two-week wall is known as the predictability barrier and it is a fundamental limitation of meteorology. Whether events are ergodic is not really relevant to the maths; even with a promise that atoms never return to their initial arrangements, the sheer size of the state space of the atmosphere will, by basic geometry, always be bigger than the amount of computation on Earth which we can assemble and bring to bear at the problem. Fun fact: chaos theory was discovered by meteorologists like Lorenz trying to figure out the correct differential equations for weather.

Think carefully. Your motte is that AI can magically turn chaotic systems into deterministic systems with simple-to-compute models; weather prediction is a counterexample. Retreating to the bailey, claiming that AI can magically initiate arbitrary societal transformations, doesn't work here because weather prediction is a counterexample to that, too; no AI will ever surmount this particular numerical obstacle, as a matter of computability theory.

I'll be honest - my current line of thought on this matter hinges around https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/algorithmic-information-dynamics/6ABDAD480E710BAD5180CED0C4822BDB, but I have not gotten around to reading it yet.

I still do have a qualm with appeals to computability theory, though, for the reason that expressiveness in terms of computability theory is distinct to expressiveness in the PL sense (link attached for the benefit of future readers).

In particular, I do not see a reason why a machine learning system could not learn to develop and build composable representations of reality, as humans do. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08381 and https://philarchive.org/rec/EVATA suggest that there is more to the story than meets the eye.

comments.author: alethkit
comments.text:
It's a formalism developed by Marcus Hutter (aka the guy behind http://prize.hutter1.net) in order to analyse certain formal properties of machine learning algorithms.

Mind you, it was developed prior to the AlexNet revolution in 2012, and it's not computable, so it's only somewhat useful as a North Star.

comments.author: marginalia
comments.text:
To be fair, multi-human software development is notoriously inefficient.

Off Conway's law alone you get O(sqrt(N)) output from N contributors, though reality is likely even worse.  The reason you hire more than 3 people is to reduce the bus factor, and to set up a pipeline of juniors to replace senior developers when they leave.

Accepting the risk of not doing so is a big part of why small startups are able to compete effectively with larger, more risk-averse organizations.

comments.author: iocompletion
comments.text:
Consider some differences, though:


Every human is unique, and this results in misunderstandings and misaligned motives. Every ai agent can start from the same place, making it more of an army of intelligent drones.

Software teams usually have senior devs leading and a mix of less senior team members contributing. AI can have every individual agent be as "intelligent" as the lead(s).


I'm not saying that's enough to overcome the challenges. Merely saying the situation is fundamentally different.
